> PulseToken is a pocket-sized hardware authenticator that shows rotating 6-digit login codes (TOTP) on a small OLED screen, so your login codes live on a separate device and not on your phone. It uses a XIAO ESP32-C3, a DS3231 real-time clock that keeps accurate time offline, three buttons to switch between accounts, and a rechargeable LiPo battery charged over USB-C. I designed a custom KiCad PCB and a 3D-printed two-part case in Onshape, with tolerances for the screen, buttons and electronics.

### 2026-10-18 – PulseToken: Week 2 journal, Oct 18–19, 2026

**6.02h**

PulseToken: Week 2 journal, Oct 18–19, 2026

Goal: finish the schematic, move to the PCB, and design a 3D-printed enclosure that fits the real board and modules.

Schematic (KiCad)

Fixed the ERC errors: added PWR_FLAG symbols on +3V3 and GND, and wired the OLED’s VCC pin, which was left floating. ERC now shows 0 violations.
Assigned footprints: 2.54 mm pin headers for the RTC, OLED and fingerprint connectors, a JST-PH 2-pin for the battery, a 0805 hand-solder resistor, and 6 mm THT tactile buttons.
Fixed J1 (RTC), which had wrongly been given the XIAO footprint.
The XIAO footprint wasn’t found in the PCB editor. I tracked down the library in my Week 1 care package and added it to the footprint library table.

PCB layout

Placed the parts: XIAO at the top edge with USB-C flush to the board edge, connectors in a column on the left, battery connector on the right, and the 3 buttons in a row along the bottom.
Drew the board outline: 52.4 × 37.4 mm.
Set track widths (0.3 mm signal, 0.5 mm power) and vias (0.8/0.4 mm).
Started routing on the back layer, since the XIAO is surface-mount and the back is free under it. Learned that a back-layer track needs a via to reach an SMD pad on the front.

Enclosure

Exported the board as a 3D model and imported it into Onshape to check sizes.
Designed the enclosure as a parametric model, so every dimension can be changed, and checked each version against the real KiCad board for collisions.
Version 1: shell, lid with a 0.2 mm lip fit, USB-C cutout, and button caps with 0.3 mm clearance.
Version 2: added a battery bay for a 402030 LiPo under the board, a wire slot, snap-fit bumps and grooves, and hold-down posts for the board.
Version 3 (final): chose the R503 fingerprint sensor, because it matches my J3 pinout and runs on 3.3 V. The AS608 sold locally needs 3.6 V+ and is too big. Used a standard 0.96" OLED.
The lid was too small for both, so I widened the case with an OLED bay (corner clips plus a 23 × 12 mm window).
Added a 25.4 mm hole for the R503’s M25 body, and made the case taller so the 19 mm sensor clears the XIAO.
Replaced the edge ledge with 4 corner supports and fences that locate the board.
Fit check result: all clear. No collisions between the case, board, battery, XIAO, sensor, OLED and caps, and all 3 caps sit over their buttons.
Final size: 75.5 × 42.4 × 34.6 mm. Exported printable models for the bottom, lid and button cap (print 3), plus a full assembly model.

Repo

Pushed everything to GitHub: CAD, printable models, PCB files, screenshots, and a README with the BOM, printing and assembly steps. All 5 repo checks pass.

Problems I hit

A missing footprint library, a footprint assigned to the wrong part, and back-layer tracks that weren’t connected without vias.
My first case left out the battery, lid retention and module mounts. Testing the design against the real parts showed this, so I redesigned it twice.
A GitHub push blocked by account permissions. Fixed with a one-time token push.

Next

Finish routing (add the via for SW1 to B3), route the remaining nets, add a GND fill, and pass DRC.
Print a tolerance test piece before printing the full case.

Tools: KiCad, Onshape, GitHub. I used Claude to help with the enclosure design and fit checks.
